Historically, libmdbx inherits the API basis from LMDB, where it is often
difficult to select flags/options and functions for the desired operation.
So it is recommend using this hints.
In tables created without the \ref MDBX_DUPSORT option, keys are always
unique. Thus always a single value corresponds to the each key, and so there
are only a few cases of changing data.
|Key exist → Error since key present          |\ref MDBX_NOOVERWRITE|Error \ref MDBX_KEYEXIST and return Present value|
|Key is absent → Error since no such key      |\ref MDBX_CURRENT    |Error \ref MDBX_NOTFOUND|
|Key is absent → Error since no such key      |\ref mdbx_del() or \ref mdbx_replace()|Error \ref MDBX_NOTFOUND|
|Key exist → Delete by key                    |\ref mdbx_del() with the parameter `data = NULL`|Deletion|

|Key exist → Delete by key with data matching check|\ref mdbx_del() with the parameter `data` filled with the value which should be match for deletion|Deletion or \ref MDBX_NOTFOUND if the value does not match|
|Delete at the current cursor position        |\ref mdbx_cursor_del() with \ref MDBX_CURRENT flag|Deletion|
|Extract (read & delete) value by the key     |\ref mdbx_replace() with zero flag and parameter `new_data = NULL`|Returning a deleted value|
In tables created with the \ref MDBX_DUPSORT (Sorted Duplicates) option, keys
may be non unique. Such non-unique keys in a key-value table may be treated
as a duplicates or as like a multiple values corresponds to keys.
|Key exist → Needn't to add new values        |\ref MDBX_NOOVERWRITE|Error \ref MDBX_KEYEXIST with returning the first value from those already present|
|Key exist → Wanna to add new values          |\ref MDBX_UPSERT     |Add one more value to the key|
|Key exist → Replace all values with a new one|\ref MDBX_UPSERT + \ref MDBX_ALLDUPS|Overwrite by single new value|
|Key is absent → Error since no such key      |\ref MDBX_CURRENT    |Error \ref MDBX_NOTFOUND|
|Key exist, Single value → Update             |\ref MDBX_CURRENT    |Update single value    |
|Key exist, Multiple values → Replace all values with a new one|\ref MDBX_CURRENT + \ref MDBX_ALLDUPS|Overwrite by single new value|
|Key exist, Multiple values → Error since it is unclear which of the values should be updated|\ref mdbx_put() with \ref MDBX_CURRENT|Error \ref MDBX_EMULTIVAL|

|Key exist, Multiple values → Update particular entry of multi-value|\ref mdbx_replace() with \ref MDBX_CURRENT + \ref MDBX_NOOVERWRITE and the parameter `old_value` filled with the value that wanna to update|Update one multi-value entry|
|Key exist, Multiple values → Update the current entry of multi-value|\ref mdbx_cursor_put() with \ref MDBX_CURRENT|Update one multi-value entry|
|Key is absent → Error since no such key      |\ref mdbx_del() or \ref mdbx_replace()|Error \ref MDBX_NOTFOUND|
|Key exist → Delete all values corresponds given key|\ref mdbx_del() with the parameter `data = NULL`|Deletion|

|Key exist → Delete particular value corresponds given key|\ref mdbx_del() with the parameter `data` filled with the value that wanna to delete, or \ref mdbx_replace() with \ref MDBX_CURRENT + \ref MDBX_NOOVERWRITE and the `old_value` parameter filled with the value that wanna to delete and `new_data = NULL`| Deletion or \ref MDBX_NOTFOUND if no such key-value pair|
|Delete one value at the current cursor position|\ref mdbx_cursor_del() with \ref MDBX_CURRENT flag|Deletion only the current entry|
|Delete all values of key at the current cursor position|\ref mdbx_cursor_del() with \ref MDBX_ALLDUPS flag|Deletion all duplicates of key (all multi-values) at the current cursor position|

lotusd uses OpenSSL. Its client offers ALPN `http/1.1`, sends SNI for host
names, and orders its TLS 1.3 suites, TLS 1.2 ciphers, groups
(`X25519MLKEM768` where OpenSSL is 3.5 or newer) and signature algorithms
like Chrome. OpenSSL cannot send GREASE values, randomize extension order,
advertise `h2` (WebSocket needs HTTP/1.1), or do ECH, so JA3/JA4
fingerprints still differ from a browser's. Dialing `wss://<IP address>`
sends no SNI, which is unusual for web traffic, so the node logs a warning.

after: `-logformat=journald` is Linux-only and writes the native journal protocol to
`/run/systemd/journal/socket`, without linking libsystemd. Selecting it enables
that sink even with `-nodebuglogfile`; it does not open the main debug file.
`-printtoconsole` and callbacks still receive readable text. An optional
`-debuglogjsonfile` continues to receive generic JSON. Startup fails explicitly
if the journal socket is unavailable. Later send failures fall back to stderr
and increment `lotus_log_journal_failures_total`; they are not counted as
successful journal writes. A successful socket send is collector acceptance,
the journal field conventions. Debug/trace map to priority 7, info to 6,
warning to 4 and error to 3. Custom metadata and typed values use `LOTUS_*`
uppercase names; the daemon never submits trusted `_` fields. Multiline/NUL
values use the length-prefixed binary representation. Oversize entries use
one sealed memfd via SCM_RIGHTS. Journal transport failures cannot indefinitely
block the logger: socket sends have a 100ms timeout and stderr fallback.

collector read. Use a durable, writable state directory for each collector:

tail databases let readers resume rather than replay the file after restart.

instead use the optional `-logtextpriority` prefix with a systemd stdout

It does not rewrite source with regular expressions. A small format parser uses
regular expressions only on captured literal bodies. It retains the complete
printf specifier in its inventory and rejects unsupported conversions rather
than silently losing width, precision or escaping.

the official 1.8.1 release provided Linux x86_64 assets only. The available
ast-grep Python wheel correctly parsed the representative nested-template
argument fixture. No claim that Comby could not implement these rules is made.
The checked-in JSON rules are reviewed semantic mappings, not inferred schemas.
They specify exact input ASTs, expected counts, event expressions, and review
notes. Whitespace may differ in input; argument tokens may not. Missing,
ambiguous, changed or unsupported mappings fail closed. Severity, category and
literal message skeletons are checked independently. Adjacent ordinary C++
string literals are supported. Raw/prefixed/dynamic formats, positional or
star-width arguments, and formatting requiring unsupported renderer behavior
remain legacy. General unsupported input appears in the rejection inventory;
a matched invalid rule aborts without changing any file. C++ macro-related
parse errors outside matched calls do not prevent conversion; parse errors
Fields such as `foo=%f` do not establish a domain name or type. New field
semantics and argument adapters require review, registry checks, compilation
and behavior tests. The tool never moves evaluation outside a logging macro or
changes the surrounding control flow. The typed logging macros' disabled-arg
and allocation contracts are independently covered by native tests and probes.
Non-call changes (field registry entries, includes, functional assertions, and
local formatting) are explicit `support_adjustments` in the rule catalog.
Commit messages must identify them separately from call conversions. The rules
preserve exact source snippets and reject ambiguous support adjustments.

manual/reviewed conversions are not retroactively described as reproducible

This standalone native test uses the real ordinary validator, VM and authenticated
transaction cost calculation. It does not start a node or establish block validity.
Coverage includes parent/child and diamond ordering, inventory TxHash versus
TxID lookup, first accepted witness retention, conflicting spends, missing versus
known-spent active inputs, actual VM rejection, byte/entry/edge/ancestor/descendant
and authenticated transaction cost caps, validation/invocation budgets, maturity
and absolute-time lock revalidation, confirmed parent survival, connected conflict
descendant removal, child-first detached resurrection, stale anchor fences and
storage failure preservation with disabled serving followed by successful retry.
The caller serializes pool access and owns the stable backend snapshot and
current-context fence. Context height and parent MTP apply to the next candidate
block. CoinLookup reads only referenced active coins; accepted parent outputs form
an overlay, and no active UTXO map is copied. Optional classify_missing distinguishes
a known active spent output from an unknown parent; absent classification means
unknown. Reconcile must run after authoritative connect/disconnect changes before
serving or mining. Its operational/stale/capacity failure retains old data while
disabling reads. The caller must retry, or discard the pool explicitly.
Limits are explicit development policy, not protocol defaults. max_ancestors and
max_descendants exclude the transaction itself. Reconcile bounds its entire input
and retries missing-parent candidates in dependency passes; exhausted validation
budget disables the old view for a caller-scheduled retry. No orphans, replacement,
persistence, relay punishment or transaction status history are implemented here.
The relay owns bounded missing-parent retries, and the coordinator owns authoritative
transition/status history. The pool computes both authenticated linear costs and
applies a local per-transaction cap. Mining must still use BuildTemplate and normal
block validation for effective/parabolic fees, block resources and commitments.

multiple inputs and other owned policies are outside this packet.

does not revoke exported bytes. A backup is a point-in-time copy and cannot
remember exports made afterward. Failed/ambiguous wallet writes require reopening
